claims.text: A blog post titled "SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi" exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ and covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
AWS CDK tied infrastructure to AWS.
Multi-cloud was nearly impossible with AWS CDK.
SST was originally built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK), which allowed developers to define infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
With CDK and CloudFormation, infrastructure code acts as a code generator producing an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources.
AWS CDK is AWS-only, while Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-prem.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python, while Pulumi supports any programming language.
AWS CDK deployments are slower due to CloudFormation, while Pulumi offers faster direct execution.
AWS CDK state management relies on a CloudFormation state file, while Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
AWS CDK supports only AWS Secrets Manager for secrets management, while Pulumi supports cross-cloud secrets.
Pulumi provides real-time debugging, while AWS CDK debugging is hard due to CloudFormation.
Pulumi does not generate an intermediary format; it treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment.

A Founding Engineer at SST said: "With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle."
Pulumi has built-in extensibility features such as custom providers and dynamic components.
Pulumi Insights provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities for deployments.
Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments.
Pulumi Cloud Deployments provides advanced deployment workflows such as faster deployment times, better rollback capabilities, and granular control.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies day one tasks and an AWS guide exists at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
An on-demand workshop titled "Getting Stated with Infrastructure as Code on AWS" exists at pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications, whose constructs/components are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation.
Once Ion is stable, it will be released as SST v3.
SST leverages Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine while also bridging Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST makes money primarily through its managed service called SST Console; the Console is optional and includes a free tier.
SST is a framework for building modern full-stack applications on your infrastructure.
Pulumi lets SST offer a faster, more flexible, and provider-agnostic infrastructure experience.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` requires no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account; the Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST keeps its state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account rather than in Pulumi Cloud.
SST v3 is the Ion-based rewrite of the SST framework.
The SST team has repeatedly said, since the rewrite shipped, that SST is built on the Pulumi engine architecture.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack.
SST can deploy applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST apps define infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST's own components, and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite code-named Ion that replaced the entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024 and has been the only supported SST architecture since.

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" says: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
The SST docs "What is SST" page says: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin's article "Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis" says SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to be defined and deployed.
Kiryl Anoshka's article "SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion" says: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."
The published platform/package.json for SST depends on `@pulumi/pulumi`, first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds and more, and a Pulumiverse Vercel provider.

The `anomalyco/sst` repository was formerly `sst/sst`, and its platform/package.json lists @pulumi/pulumi, @pulumi/aws, @pulumi/cloudflare, @pulumi/command, @pulumi/docker-build, @pulumi/random, @pulumi/tls, and @pulumiverse/vercel as direct dependencies.
The Pulumi engine diffs desired versus actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations.
`sst deploy` reads `sst.config.ts`, resolves SST's own components, and those components compile into Pulumi resource declarations.
Terraform-bridged providers, via Pulumi's Terraform bridge, translate each resource into cloud API calls.
Pulumi's engine handles dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs in SST.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's provider ecosystem with the Pulumi engine.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API works by embedding Pulumi programs inside teams' own tools in the same embedded way.
The Terraform provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
Nitric's docs state: "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
Official Nitric providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.
Nitric is a cloud-agnostic application framework.
Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud, and its Pulumi provider (DefangLabs/pulumi-defang) takes a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`.
Nitric and Defang, like SST, expose a narrower, more opinionated interface while relying on the Pulumi engine and its provider bridge underneath.
Most SST users never write Pulumi code and work entirely in SST's component model.
Resources without a dedicated SST construct can be defined directly in Pulumi and deployed as part of the same SST app, because SST's constructs compile to Pulumi resources.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` npm package receives roughly 796,000 downloads per week (796,291 for the week of September 5-11, 2026).
SST's team page credits the same team behind opencode, an open source AI coding agent.
opencode (anomalyco/opencode) now has more GitHub stars than SST itself.
opencode has grown quickly since launch.
SST's dependency on the Pulumi engine has not changed and SST's release cadence has not changed since the team's attention broadened to opencode.
SST doesn't invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state; its Terraform providers are bridged through the Pulumi engine.
Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state; policy as code provides guardrails enforced centrally; components allow sharing infrastructure patterns across an organization.
Pulumi features such as Pulumi Cloud, policy as code and components can be used alongside SST without leaving the engine SST already uses.
SST doesn't expose cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure sharing across more than one application on its own.
A blog post exists at /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/ titled 'AWS CDK vs Pulumi: Why SST Chose Pulumi', telling SST's move off CDK from SST's side.
A docs page exists at /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/ titled 'How Pulumi IaC Works'.
A blog post exists at /blog/any-terraform-provider/ titled 'Introducing: Support For Using Any Terraform Provider with Pulumi'; docs page /docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers/ exists.
Docs pages exist at /docs/iac/concepts/pulumi-cloud/, /docs/iac/concepts/policy/, /docs/iac/concepts/components/, and /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/.
